Title: Why we are against card fixes

Messages.Author: Legbiter
Messages.Body:
We always seem to be reacting to other peoples' posts and doubtless that
makes us look reactionary. So I thought it might be helpful if I just
summarised what our views are about card fixes, and the philosophy from
which they spring. "Us" means me, Jason and Chris that I know of, also
possibly Michael Beer's evil twin, but this posting is personal and I
haven't consulted the other guys about it. Still, I think they will agree
with most of this post.

My view is that Jyhad is a beautiful and balanced game. Where lack of
clarity exists, it can often be resolved by reference to the role-playing
game. I believe that Jyhad has a great future because it is, objectively,
the best TCG technically, and it has the coolest background [everyone
wants to live forever and have passionate physical relations with
attractive members of the individually-desired but usually opposite
gender]. Currently, these facts are under-appreciated by the license
holders, but this will change as Wizards' cash-flow improves [buying TSR
can't have been cheap]. In the meantime it should be the overriding
concern of all of us to bring in new players and to maintain the game as
best we can. Given that Jyhad is a complex game, this will usually mean
simplifying and streamlining the rules, and CERTAINLY NOT introducing new
rules unsupportable by card text.

I am against card fixes IN GENERAL, UNLESS there is an overwhelmingly good
reason for instituting one. Overwhelmingly good should include a return
[where appropriate] to the literal wording of the card, and should NEVER
involve a rewording of the card. Or, there should be clear proof that a
particular card is so seriously unbalanced that it threatens the integrity
of the game. This DOES NOT mean that a card hosing a particular deck style
is a candidate for banning. Nor does it mean that powerful cards in
general should be banned. Actually, we all agree with this, if we think
about it .... no-one agonises about the desirability of WWEF or Blood
Doll, though I doubt there's a deck on the planet that doesn't contain
these ..... And lest this general opposition seem a tad reactionary, I beg
you to believe that it springs from observation of the effects of
card-fixes/bans on Magic, and fear that the same process is already
encroaching upon Jyhad.

I am also against certain card fixes IN PARTICULAR, on the grounds that I
think the past fix is wrong, or that the proposed fix is unnecessary.

Examples of bad fixes I'm against:
Rutor's hand damage as preventable by combat cards, Merril's ability and
indeed anything except Tears of Kephran. This is a classic example of a
bad fix. The card text is absolutely clear, and it means that you can't
prevent the damage except with the blood tears. It's also bad from the
role-playing point of view. You rip out an eye, rip off your hand and then
expect to prevent it with a combat manoeuver or your nice new leather
jacket???? Pur-lease!!! In fact, how on Caine's EARTH did this fix ever
happen??? Presumably because somebody playing a Tremere deck moaned and
whined enough so that the rules team acted. It should be an example to us
all to be REAL careful about future fixes.

Return to Innocence:
We've been round the houses on this one. It is a big bleed card, with a
big cost. It potentially gives ANY deck, and not just the [spit!] Ventrue,
Brujah, Malkavians, Toreadors and Tremere the potential to be decks of
maximum bleedy harm. Contrary to what others have written, it is NOT a
sure-fire oust. I actually believe that, if anything, this card REBALANCES
the game, because it makes it worthwhile to bring out big vampires, and it
gives a bleed dimension to the otherwise bleed-challenged Gangrel and
Nosferatu. Those reluctant to accept this might like to check out Robert
Goudie's wise words on cycles of RtI-ness and weenie decks in LA,
reachable through Rulemonger's page.

Tomb of Rameses III:
We're not achieving consensus on this one at all. I think some of the
arguments against it are unworthy of this group - that it's a
something-for-nothing card [so is Art Scam, Ascendance, etc] just doesn't
fly. But once again, the good thing about this card is that it gives you
the chance to get out big vamps. And there ARE defenses against it ....
which we've talked about, without so far once mentioning Memory's Fading
Glimpse. One of the main ones of course is that being such a good card it
is likely that at least one other person at your table wants to play it.
Think about this one, guys 'n' gals .. those of you who responded when I
made this point before didn't always see the difference between how good
it is to be the ONLY person with Tomb in play, and how bad it is to
realise that everyone including you, but not your predator, has stacked up
their hands with this card ....

Thoughts Betrayed:
Once again, I think people are not seeing how this card instantly puts
extra value on Allies, Retainers and Weapons, which in other posts we are
all agreeing need a boost. "Hah! Foul fiend of Darkness! You think to use
your Eldritch powers of the Mind on me???? Well meet the renowned debating
team of Smith and Wesson! <BLAM! BLAM!>"

And I must admit, as this debate has progressed my opposition to card
fixes has hardened. For example, I WAS in favour of the CW change, till
James Coupe launched his [for me] absolutely devastating counter-argument.
Even the Dragos fix now seems to me OTT ... after all, it only affects a
coupla combat cards [Lightning reflexes and Eldritch Glimmer], you have to
play TWO master cards on him before it becomes a problem, even then he is
vulnerable to Thoughts Betrayed, and it's not like combat decks are
sweeping the tournament board under the current dispensation, is it???

Alright, well that was the manifesto of the Marinus van der Lubbe
International Fireboming Society, posted in the interests of Increased
Brotherly Love and general fuzzy-feelingness by Legbiter*, BSc [Edin:
Summa Cum Laude], PhD, MRPPBHSIWM [Most Ridiculous Post Peter Bajika Has
Seen in Weeks Medal... and I hope to get a bar and oak-leaves on that
before the year is out .... hehehe ....].

*In Reality an Ancient Malkavian, but my daylight hours are spent in the
pursuit of a complex role-playing game in which i'm a human research
scientist active in the field of genetic disease. This fantasy character
can be reached at: james.m...@port.ac.uk.

Messages.Author: James Coupe
Messages.Body:
In article <not.available-2...@sm1-132.hs.port.ac.uk>,
Legbiter <not.av...@your.security.clearance> writes

>Even the Dragos fix now seems to me OTT ... after all, it only affects a
>coupla combat cards [Lightning reflexes and Eldritch Glimmer], you have to
>play TWO master cards on him before it becomes a problem,

Not a fix. The intention of Dragos is to avoid the COST of playing a
combat card ie that little thing in the blood drop. The fact that
Lightning Reflexes and Eldritch Glimmer don't work with it is therefore
no problem - that is bringing it back to card text. Indeed, it never
violates card text - it was just meant to clear it up for people who
didn't realise that the X didn't count as a cost (in most cases, the
distinction is unnecessary).

Messages.Author: PDB6
Messages.Body:
Legbiter wrote:
"My view is that Jyhad is a beautiful and balanced game. Where lack of clarity
exists, it can often be resolved by reference to the role-playing game."

But those of us who hold no stock in the RPG and play Jyhad simply because it
is a well designed and strategically interesting game have no wish to rely on
such sketchy sources. If this were the case, then my Nosferatu certainly
couldn't use WWEF, now could they...

"Given that Jyhad is a complex game, this will usually mean simplifying and
streamlining the rules, and CERTAINLY NOT introducing new rules unsupportable
by card text."

While a noble thought, the fact that the three expansions (one might notice
that there are no cards in the original basic set that people complain about as
busted, just wallpapery) introduced overpowered and poorly playtested cards to
the mix necessitate the need for such fixes. Add to this the fact that there
will never actually be any new cards added to the mix to change things, this is
all we have.

"I am against card fixes IN GENERAL, UNLESS there is an overwhelmingly good
reason for instituting one."

For most of us around here, an overwhelmingly good reason is extremely negative
effect on the game enviornment as typified by Tomb of Ramses III and Return to
Innocence.

"I am also against certain card fixes IN PARTICULAR, on the grounds that I
think the past fix is wrong, or that the proposed fix is unnecessary."

Most exisiting fixes were made due to either a misprint on the card (making
them necessary) or ambiguious card text (also making them necessary). Very
few, if any, cards have been officially fixed due to balance problems.

"Tomb of Rameses III:
We're not achieving consensus on this one at all. I think some of the
arguments against it are unworthy of this group - that it's a
something-for-nothing card [so is Art Scam, Ascendance, etc] just doesn't fly."

But yes, it does. The cards you mentioned (Art Scam and Ascendance) give you
an advantage based on a cost in comparison to all the other cards in the game.
Art Scam, for example, gives you one pool for an action. There are many other
compareable cards that have a very similar effect for a very similar cost.
Tomb, however, gives you advantages far greater than any compareable card (in
terms of speed, pool gain, and risk in use). Tomb is not a game destroying
card. It is, however, certainly overpowered (in terms of cost/effect) and
easily leeds to a great deal of abuse that was not prevelant before its
existance, and consequently has a much greater effect on the game enviornement
than justified.

"Thoughts Betrayed:
Once again, I think people are not seeing how this card instantly puts extra
value on Allies, Retainers and Weapons, which in other posts we are all
agreeing need a boost."

But having to build a deck that relies on useless Allies and weapons just to
(hopefully) combat TB is simply asking to be killed.

The real problem with TB is not that it is completely overpowered, just that it
is a completely unwarranted and unacceptable effect for _any_ card of _any_
cost.

"[Edin:Summa Cum Laude], PhD, MRPPBHSIWM [Most Ridiculous Post Peter Bajika Has
Seen in Weeks Medal... and I hope to get a bar and oak-leaves on that before
the year is out .... hehehe ....]."

Just keep on working hard, and one day your dreams will be realized (Man, can't
_anyone_ spell my name right?).

Messages.Author: PDB6
Messages.Body:
Jasper Philips wrote:
"Rotschrek? For some reason I thought there were more..."

I don't think that Rotshreck was changed as it was due to play balance issues,
I think it was due to the ambiguousness of the card text. It is possible that
the original purpose of the card was to screw the guy about to _take_ the aggro
damage, but in reality, this seems kind of unlikely and pointless (or
incredibly subtle and brilliant on the part of the game designers, but I just
don't see it...) and they probably would not have made the card to do this in
the first place.

As it is, it seems likely that the original intention was as anti-aggro damage
hoser (although this does not make any sense in terms of the game world, it
fits the logic of the Masters as hosers scheme that was a part of the basic
set, much like Frenzy and Masquerade Endangered) and the card was very poorly
worded. In the final evaluation, it seemed that the original intention of the
card was to hose aggro-damage use, and thus the ruling.

I agree that the card pretty much says the exact opposite and that it being an
aggro-hoser is pretty non sensical (Basillia yelling "My Hands!" and freaking
out and all), but again I maintain that it seems very unlikely that the card's
original intent was as a Master Out Of Turn aggro user bonus ("here look at my
mighty claws...NOW GO DIRECTLY TO TORPOR!!!! BWAHAHAHAHA!!!") and that it was
intended to be an aggro-hoser but was worded extremely poorly.



Messages.Author: PDB6
Messages.Body:
Legbiter wrote:
"I think the original intention of this card was to save the bacon of a vampire
who was about to get burned in combat. This is essentially what Rotschreck does
in the RPG - the vamp bottles out completely and runs as far as its undead legs
will carry it. So it puts a vamp [usually yours] in torpor, 'stead of it being
chewed up."

I the original Jyhad set, it was _very_ difficult to burn someone (due to the
old aggro rules), and I find it hard to fathom that they designed such an
obscure single use card to deal with being burned. In the original set, pretty
much the only ways to get burned were Flamethrower, Dragonsbreath rounds,
Sengir Dagger/Pot, and the ever sketchy Pot/Pro combat, and even those were a
hard way to burn someone.

and Eric Petterson wrote:
"Also of some use for Gangrel against S:CE (but only when blocking)."

Yes, if Rotchreck is used as written (sends the guy about to _take_ aggro to
torpor), it is a good anti S:CE card for a gangrel intercept deck, but again,
it seems unlikely that the original designers of the game had this though, as
if they had, then why not make a less obscure way for the Gangrel to deal with
it? Why not an offensive use anti-S:CE card for the Gangrel, as they
originally were envisioned as the premeire combat clan (which turned out to
simply not be the case)? I suspect that the impact that S:CE has had upon the
game was probably not fully understood at the time of the original release, and
thus anti-S:CE cards were really not a design focus. In the original set, the
only really specific anti-S:CE card there was was Immortal Grapple, and that
was Rare(notice how in Sabbat there is much less S:CE and Immortal Grapple is
Uncommon--I suspect by the time of Sabbat they had figured out their error...).

Both of these are good points, but still I suspect that when designed,
Rotschreck was probably meant to be a aggro hoser (like Frenzy is a MOOT weapon
hoser and Masquerade Endangered is a MOOT Hunting hoser) and they just woorded
it very poorly.


